This means that for anyone who believes the dollar depreciates by more than 7% annually, the subsidies haven't kept pace with the dollar's depreciation; and even at a 6% depreciation rate, they've only barely kept pace. Given this decline in mining rewards, a slowdown or even contraction in Bitcoin mining is to be expected. Unless there's a significant reversal in this metric, this trend could continue indefinitely. This pattern is also reflected in the significant decrease in Bitcoin mining difficulty over the past ten months. Bitcoin's mining difficulty reached an all-time high on October 30, 2025, and 305 days later, it has yet to recover or surpass that level. This is the second longest period during which Bitcoin's difficulty has failed to reach a new all-time high. The longest such period was from August 1, 2011, to July 30, 2012, taking 363 days to reach a new all-time high. That decline was accompanied by the largest price correction in Bitcoin's history, with the price falling from $30 in June 2011 to $2 in November 2011, a 94% pullback. The third longest period of difficulty began on May 16, 2021, and lasted 252 days until January 23, 2022, when the difficulty reached a new all-time high. That round occurred after China banned mining, a significant event as China at the time accounted for a large share of Bitcoin mining, forcing many miners to liquidate their operations, sell their machines, or move them overseas. The need for liquidation likely also meant selling some of their Bitcoin holdings, triggering a sharp drop in Bitcoin's price. What's special about this current difficulty decline is that, unlike the first and third longest periods, it didn't occur after a dramatic event. Bitcoin's maximum retracement from its October 2025 all-time high is currently only 54%, far lower than the 95% in 2011; nor has it been accompanied by a major regulatory event affecting Bitcoin miners like in 2021. However, the difficulty has already dropped significantly, and if it takes another two months to recover, this will be the longest period of difficulty decline in Bitcoin history. March 14, 2024: Peak Bitcoin Mining Rewards Another noteworthy fact is that, with two years and four months having passed in this fifth Bitcoin cycle, the mining reward per block is 3.125 bitcoins, and the daily mining reward in US dollars has not yet exceeded the highest level set in the previous cycle—that was on March 14, 2024, when the price was $73,800 and the reward per block was 6.25 bitcoins. On that day, assuming 144 blocks were produced, the total mining reward was equivalent to $65 million ($144 blocks × $73,800 per bitcoin × 6.25 bitcoins per block). March 14th was the highest reward of the previous cycle, and for the mining reward to match this cycle after the halving, the price needs to reach $147,600. Since the highest price this cycle only reached $126,000, we haven't seen a day with a higher dollar-denominated block reward value this cycle. If the price fails to reach $147,600 before the next halving, this will be the first cycle in which the daily mining reward fails to exceed the previous cycle's high. March 14, 2024, may even go down in history as the day with the highest Bitcoin reward value ever. With each upcoming halving, the price needs to double again to match the market capitalization rewarded on that day. If the Bitcoin price doesn't reach $147,600 in the fifth cycle before the next halving, then to surpass the value of March 14, 2024, in the sixth cycle (2028-2032), the price would need to reach $295,200; in the seventh cycle (2032-2036), it would need to reach $590,400; and in the eighth cycle, it would need to reach $1,180,800. The required price will continue to double every four years. I'm not suggesting that any of these values ​​are unattainable; I'm simply saying that they might not be achievable. And if they are, March 14, 2024, will forever remain the most valuable day in Bitcoin mining history. More specifically, even if one of these cycles surpasses the value of March 14, 2024, there will inevitably come another day when its mining reward value will never be surpassed, because Bitcoin's value cannot double every four years indefinitely. It's hard to imagine its market capitalization doubling every four years once the whole world uses Bitcoin as currency. If it's not March 14, 2024, then some other future date will mark the peak of Bitcoin mining. Whether the peak of Bitcoin mining has already occurred can only be answered by time; but a stronger argument is that such a peak will inevitably occur at some point. By then, Bitcoin mining will have peaked in both capital investment and electricity consumption, but mining difficulty will recover and likely continue to rise as mining equipment efficiency improves. Peak Electricity Consumption The most direct test of this hypothesis comes from Cambridge University's estimates of Bitcoin's electricity consumption. Preliminary data released by the Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance (CCAL) indicates that the annualized electricity demand for Bitcoin mining in December 2025 was approximately 190 terawatt-hours (TWh). Subsequently, the Cambridge Bitcoin Electricity Consumption Index (CBEE) declined significantly, with the mid-2026 estimate falling back to the high end of the 130 TWh range. This provides a clear empirical test for the hypothesis. The annualized level of approximately 190 TWh in December 2025 may prove to be the peak of Bitcoin's electricity consumption rate. If the best-in-class Cambridge estimate subsequently continues to rise above this level, then this specific assertion will be disproven. However, the decline since December is consistent with the broader argument discussed above: reward revenue growth is slowing, difficulty has been unusually low for an extended period, and the amount of electricity that miners can profitably consume is beginning to shrink.

AI Accelerator

Another reason to believe we may have witnessed the peak of Bitcoin mining is the rise of AI as a major source of data center and electricity demand. Over the past four years, the number of data centers has surged to meet the explosive demand for AI, providing Bitcoin miners with another lucrative revenue stream. Rumors and observations of major Bitcoin mining companies suggest a massive shift in mining infrastructure towards AI data centers.

This indicates that Bitcoin mining has entered a new era: it is no longer the only way to monetize cheap and discarded energy, as AI can now also compete for these resources; and the massive investments in AI may be accelerating the decline in Bitcoin mining capital expenditures and electricity consumption. After years of investment in Bitcoin mining infrastructure, much of the discarded energy used for Bitcoin mining is now more sophisticated and better connected to the internet, making it more suitable for AI data centers.

The key difference between AI data centers and Bitcoin mining is that Bitcoin's difficulty adjustment makes it a zero-sum game, while AI data centers are a positive-sum game. As AI increases user productivity, they will continue to invest more in it, demanding increasingly larger workloads. However, Bitcoin mining is competing for a shrinking Bitcoin pie, halving in size every four years. Difficulty adjustments further ensure that only the most efficient miners can profit, and as more miners join and rewards halve without a corresponding doubling of revenue, profit margins will only become thinner. AI, on the other hand, could bring huge productivity gains across countless industries, thus supporting ever-increasing demand. Bitcoin miners now face a dilemma: declining expected returns from Bitcoin halvings versus potentially exponentially increasing returns from AI productivity gains. It's possible that AI will ultimately prove to be a huge bubble, with a large portion of these data center expenditures becoming waste. Chinese AI models appear capable of achieving results similar to US models with minimal energy and processing power costs. If most AI spending ultimately proves to be a wasteful misinvestment (unlikely), miners will return to Bitcoin mining, but this won't change a fundamental judgment: Bitcoin mining will peak at some point in the future. Transaction Fees To simplify the analysis, this article omits one factor: the growth of transaction fees. For most of Bitcoin's history, fees have only accounted for a small portion of miners' revenue. If fees were to rise significantly, the following analysis might become invalid, as mining rewards (including subsidies and fees) could rise to levels exceeding those of the previous cycle. However, the Bitcoin network has grown significantly, while fees denominated in Bitcoin have remained flat or even decreased over time; with the continued development of Layer 2 solutions, it's likely that fees will not rise significantly, and total mining rewards will never exceed the levels of the previous cycle. In my view, the idea that Bitcoin transaction fees need to reach a certain "security budget" is largely misleading. I don't believe fees need to grow to any specific level to ensure network security; a network is secure because there's the possibility of paying fees to circumvent mining censorship, not because fees have reached a certain level. The impact: If this assumption holds true, it's not a problem for Bitcoin. Bitcoin's supply continues to grow as planned, and as more people understand this, and understand that the supply of all other monetary assets is growing much faster, demand for Bitcoin is likely to continue to increase. We will enter a new era: Bitcoin is growing, while the scale of Bitcoin mining is shrinking. The impact on Bitcoin mining is that its scale is likely to shrink over time, and its profitability may also decline. This could very well lead more Bitcoin holders to shift their investments from mining to directly buying Bitcoin, which is likely to be bullish for the price. As Bitcoin's energy consumption decreases, the hysteria surrounding Bitcoin's energy consumption is likely to subside, as is the large amount of negative reporting. This is also bullish for the price. The actionable takeaway is: if you understand Bitcoin's value proposition, buy Bitcoin directly. If you have cheap electricity and the ability to build mining facilities, then turn to AI data centers. Conclusion: Bitcoin mining once had a structural long-term tailwind: the rate at which the monetization of block rewards increased far faster than the rate at which the number of Bitcoins was reduced by halvings. This tailwind has disappeared. Despite a 2.56-fold increase in the average Bitcoin price this cycle, nominal block reward revenue was only 28% higher than the previous cycle; after accounting for the depreciation of the US dollar, this increase is close to zero. Meanwhile, mining difficulty is experiencing its second-longest period of failure to reach new highs in history, Cambridge's estimated electricity consumption has fallen sharply from its potential peak in late 2025, and AI is increasing the opportunity cost of high-quality mining infrastructure. Bitcoin's fundamentals suggest it may continue to grow, but Bitcoin mining and its electricity consumption may have already peaked.

data.title: The ideal has come to an end: Why is the crypto industry collectively becoming homogenized?
data.description:
Written by: @100y_eth   Translated by: Saoirse, Foresight News

Most experiments in crypto idealism have come to an end

"Decentralization," readable-writable-ownable, Web3, community ownership, do not be evil, cyber nation, code is law, trustless verification only, creator economy, pluralism, future governance…

These concepts are no longer just technical terms. They have attracted a large number of idealistic practitioners to the blockchain industry, who believe they can build a more open, free, and fair digital world.

Everyone has different visions for the future, but there is a consensus within the industry: blockchain has the ability to reshape the existing order.

Countless practitioners have dedicated themselves to this field, putting their ideals into practice, giving rise to a large number of experiments, protocols, and services, and continuously expanding the boundaries of the ecosystem: DAO, fan tokens, ve (3,3), NFT, intellectual property NFT, music NFT, Bitcoin inscriptions and runes, Bitcoin Layer 2 network, Play-2-Earn, Move-2-Earn, metaverse, on-chain games, game guilds, decentralized social networking, decentralized identity DID, on-chain reputation, soul-bound token SBT, algorithmic stablecoins, restaking, InfoFi, Ethereum killer, application chain, modular blockchain, zkEVM, Rollup-as-a-Service, intent transaction, chain abstraction, DePIN, decentralized energy, regenerative finance ReFi, decentralized scientific research DeSci, data market, decentralized AI computing power... However, regrettably, the vast majority of these experiments have failed. Numerous projects have failed; some representative examples are listed below. This chart shows the Bitcoin network transaction fee trend from 2023 to 2026. Transaction fees surged multiple times during the inscription craze, then declined after 2025, and the network congestion caused by inscriptions largely subsided. Inscriptions, ordinal NFTs, and runes store arbitrary data using Bitcoin's Segregated Witness and OP-RETURN transaction fields. At the time, the market touted the possibility of issuing tokens and NFTs with Bitcoin, and related hype remained high. In 2023, inscriptions drove up Bitcoin network transaction fees, with some even arguing that these fees could offset the shortfall caused by the Bitcoin block reward halving. However, today, their impact on Bitcoin network fees is almost negligible. Ordinal Maxi Biz, once a leading ordinal NFT project, reached a peak price of 1.5 Bitcoins, but recently traded for only about 0.018 Bitcoins. Magic Eden, once the largest Bitcoin NFT exchange, ceased its Bitcoin NFT trading operations in March of this year. Bitcoin Layer 2 Networks: Technologies like Taproot and BitVM led the market to believe that programmable, scalable Layer 2 networks could be built on top of Bitcoin's high security, attracting numerous projects to secure funding from leading venture capital firms. However, the overall ecosystem is currently performing poorly. BOB, the Bitcoin Layer 2 project with the highest locked value, has seen its total locked value plummet by 96.6% from its peak, leaving only $9.24 million. Corn, BEVM, and Lorenzo have completed their complete transformations, while Botanix has shut down entirely. A comparison of the TVL (Total Value Locked) ratios of Ethereum and other public chains from 2021 to 2026 shows that despite the rise of many competing public chains, Ethereum still maintains the highest share of total value locked in DeFi, and its dominant position in the industry remains unbroken. Many emerging public chains and Layer 2 networks claim to surpass Ethereum in scalability, incentive mechanisms, contract security, and market operation strategies. However, many projects have failed to find a product-market fit, becoming "ghost chains" without real users. Aside from Binance Chain, Tron, Solana, and Base, which have accumulated real users and established a viable business model, the vast majority of other public blockchains have failed to gain a significant market share from Ethereum. The infrastructure sector was the hottest infrastructure sector in 2022-2023. Starting with the Data Availability Layer (DA), the market saw the emergence of shared sorters, Rollup as a Service (Rollup as a Service), and various Rollup solutions. The design philosophy of modularity itself is not flawed; Arbitrum, Base, and Robinhood Chain are still operating stably. However, most of the modular startups that gained significant popularity back then either chose to transform their business models or went bankrupt. That wave of modularity can be considered a failed industry experiment. The chart shows the total value locked (TVL) in the restaking sector from 2024 to 2026. This sector's TVL peaked at nearly $30 billion before experiencing a significant pullback, a more drastic decline compared to other DeFi sectors. Restaking refers to the reuse of tokens already staked on a PoS public chain to provide economic security for other protocols. EigenLayer pioneered this sector, followed by Symbiotic, Karak, and other public chain ecosystems like Babylon and Solayer. The total value locked in this sector peaked at $30 billion, but has now fallen back to approximately $8 billion. While the total value locked (TVL) remains substantial, the narrative surrounding it has cooled significantly: the market possesses abundant reusable security resources, but the business demand for such security is extremely scarce. EigenLayer has undergone a soft transformation, focusing on EigenCloud, an AI agent-oriented platform; Symbiotic has shifted towards high-performance public chains, and Karak has transformed into a collateral trading platform. This chart shows the market capitalization trend of Terra UST from 2021 to 2026. UST's market capitalization once surged to nearly $20 billion before completely collapsing to zero, an event that made algorithmic stablecoins almost taboo in the crypto industry. The goal of algorithmic stablecoins is to move away from full asset collateralization and create more capital-efficient decentralized on-chain currencies. UST (now USTC) in the Terra ecosystem is the most well-known example, with a peak circulating supply exceeding $18 billion, ranking among the top ten crypto assets. However, external attacks combined with design flaws in the underlying mechanism caused the token price to plummet to zero, leading to the collapse of the entire Terra ecosystem. Other algorithmic stablecoin projects such as FEI, Iron, and ESD also all failed. FRAX initially used an algorithmic mechanism but later switched to a fiat-collateralized model.

NFT, Blockchain Games, and the Metaverse Ecosystem

The bar chart shows the monthly transaction volume trend of OpenSea. During the NFT boom in 2022, the platform's monthly transaction volume once surged to nearly $5 billion. After the boom subsided, the transaction volume remained at a low level for a long time, symbolizing that the NFT bull market was like a short-lived dream.

NFTs once broke out of their niche and entered the mainstream. They emerged on Ethereum in 2021 and then spread to the Solana and Klaytn ecosystems. The prices of top collectibles skyrocketed, followed by a collective collapse.

NFTs once broke out of their niche and entered the mainstream. They emerged on Ethereum in 2021 and then spread to the Solana and Klaytn ecosystems. The prices of top collectibles skyrocketed, followed by a collective collapse.

CryptoPunks fell from 125 ETH to 32 ETH; BAYC from 150 ETH to 8 ETH; Pudgy Penguins from 35 ETH to 3.8 ETH; and Azuki from 30 ETH to 0.8 ETH. Leading NFT platform OpenSea saw its monthly transaction volume shrink from a peak of $5 billion to approximately $30 million. The core concept of P2E (Play-to-Earn) is that players own an in-game economy, earning crypto assets and sharing in the ecosystem's value by participating. However, for the model to be sustainable, the game must create real economic value or generate voluntary player payments. Neither of these has been achieved, leading to the collapse of the vast majority of projects. Axie Infinity, which popularized P2E, reached a peak of 6.5 million monthly active wallets and $103.8 million in transaction fees; now, it has fewer than 100,000 monthly active users and less than $50,000 in monthly transaction fees. Alongside the P2E boom, land NFT metaverse projects like Sandbox and Decentraland experienced a period of immense popularity. However, Sandbox land NFT prices plummeted by 99%, from a peak of approximately $15,000 to just $50. Projects like StepN and Sweat, which allowed users to earn money while playing, quickly lost their luster. AAA blockchain games like Star Atlas and Otherside never officially launched; the concept of fully blockchain-based gaming also failed to attract a large number of ordinary users. The blockchain gaming sector, once considered the future of the gaming industry, has largely failed in its implementation. Decentralized Social Networking and Information Finance

The chart shows the changes in Farcaster's daily active users, posting/interaction/linking volume. After peaking in March 2026, the platform's daily active users and on-chain interaction scale continued to decline, and the market enthusiasm for decentralized social networking gradually cooled down.

Decentralized social networking is the most direct practical application of the "user-owned internet" concept. It promises users control over their own social relationship graph, permissionless access, and censorship resistance, giving rise to projects such as Farcaster, Lens, and DeSo. However, apart from the users brought in by token incentives in the short term, projects find it difficult to retain real users, and overall activity has declined significantly. InfoFi, pioneered by Kaito, links online attention, content creation, and economic rewards. While it initially produced a significant amount of high-quality content, subsequent rampant practice of artificially inflating traffic for profit led to a proliferation of spam. After the X platform shut down its related interfaces, Kaito's Yaps, Cookie DAO's Snaps, and Wallchain's Quacks all ceased operations. The vision envisioned by crypto idealists has not materialized in the short term. However, Bitcoin has already been regarded as digital gold by some in the market; the traditional financial industry has also begun to actively adopt blockchain as the next-generation financial infrastructure. Blockchain has finally found its own product-market fit. The Era of On-Chain Experimentation Ends: Crypto Projects Shutting Down or Transforming in 2026

The industry previously generally believed that the various idealistic experiments would have largely ended by 2024-2025. The market shifted from grand narratives to tracks like stablecoins and asset tokenization, where business models were easier to implement, and the ideals of the previous cycle gradually faded from public view.

However, the reality continued to deteriorate: innovation had stagnated, capital and traffic began to withdraw, but older projects could still barely keep operating by relying on remaining funding and business inertia. Recently, however, these older projects have truly reached their end, with many initiating transformations or shutting down altogether.

As the table shows, in 2026, centralized exchanges, data tools, public chains, layer 2 networks, infrastructure, DeFi, games, and NFTs—almost the entire crypto space—experienced a wave of closures and transformations. The idealistic experiments of the crypto world have truly come to an end. The digital world envisioned by idealists has ultimately failed to materialize. The market has formed a barbell-shaped bipolar structure, with sectors converging. This scatter plot shows the year-on-year changes in key indicators, with the market moving towards both ends: speculative and traditional financial RWA sectors saw significant data surges, while traditional crypto sectors such as native on-chain DeFi, NFTs, and restaking experienced substantial data contractions, indicating a decline in the middle sectors. After countless on-chain experiments failed, the crypto industry evolved into a polarized barbell structure. One end caters to users' speculative demands; the other end supports the stable business needs of the real economy. Those native on-chain businesses in the middle, with unclear risk-return characteristics, have performed poorly in various operating data, due to three core reasons: **Lack of Product-Market Fit:** As mentioned earlier, the vast majority of on-chain products have not successfully implemented Proof-of-Function (PMF). Some seemingly successful cases, upon closer examination, were merely a false boom fueled by early airdrop activities. Products that can truly create value and continuously provide utility to users are extremely rare. **Risk-Reward Ratio Continues to Deteriorate:** With the crypto market weakening, users are gradually distinguishing which models are feasible and which are merely pseudo-demands. Expected returns from ordinary DeFi mining have declined significantly. Previously, stablecoin mining could achieve annualized returns of 15-20%; now, even 5-10% annualized returns are extremely difficult to obtain. The appeal of the middle-ground sector has completely disappeared. Users are divided into two groups: either turning to RWA, accepting low-risk returns of 3-7%; or flocking to Meme Coin, perpetual contracts, and prediction markets, taking on high risks to seek excess returns. **Increased Risk of Hacking:** With the iterative upgrades of large-scale AI models, on-chain hacking incidents are becoming increasingly frequent. The already shrunken expected returns, coupled with the risk of principal theft, further weaken the appeal of ordinary on-chain products. Data from two extreme sectors bucked the trend and rose, as if the bear market had never arrived. Some businesses are highly tied to crypto market conditions; others have built independent business models, unaffected by token price fluctuations. This has created a barbell-shaped development pattern for the entire industry. Speculative Demand: Speculation is not unique to the crypto industry. While speculative targets constantly change, human nature remains constant. From tulip mania and land speculation to stocks and cryptocurrencies, speculative demand has always existed. The characteristics of smart contracts, on-chain transparency, and instant settlement make blockchain a prime vehicle for speculative behavior. After the decline in the appeal of traditional DeFi, a large number of traditional DeFi users have flocked to speculative sectors, with representative categories including Meme coins, prediction markets, and decentralized perpetual contract (DEX) contracts. The market demand for Meme Coin has continued since Dogecoin in 2013: DOGE→SHIB→BONK→PEPE. In 2024, the Solana ecosystem's WIF, POPCAT, MEW, GOAT, and FARTCOIN sparked a Meme Coin craze. What truly reshaped the industry landscape was shturl.c, launched in 2024, which allows anyone to issue Meme Coins with a single click. The bar chart shows the revenue trend of the shturl.c platform. Even with market fluctuations, the revenue of this Meme coin issuing platform has remained high for a long time. In August and September 2026, revenue even surged to over $2 million, demonstrating the continued popularity of the Meme sector. While spot DEX trading volume has plummeted by nearly 80% in the past year, shturl.c's revenue has shown remarkable resilience, more than doubling from its low point in the past month. The platform has implemented a "graduation" mechanism: once a token's market capitalization reaches a threshold, it migrates from the glue curve to the AMM liquidity pool. The percentage of tokens that successfully graduate has increased from an average of less than 1% to over 3%. The image shows the daily spot trading volume breakdown for July. Meme Coin (bright yellow) initially had a very high share, and although it gradually declined, it remains the most traded asset on the chain, exceeding the trading volume of ETH (stablecoins) and tokenized assets. The newly launched Robinhood Chain was initially positioned as a public chain for tokenizing real-world assets. However, the vast majority of its trading volume comes from Meme Coin. Blockworks statistics show that more than half of the spot trading volume after launch was contributed by Meme Coin. Ironically, Meme Coin has become the growth engine of this RWA-focused public chain. The chart shows the net revenue trend of the Fomo platform. Starting in June 2025, revenue surged in the second half of 2026, confirming the rapid expansion of the Meme trading platform. Also noteworthy is the Fomo platform, created by former dYdX employees. It has a low barrier to entry, allows for quick discovery of Meme coin projects, features a social news feed, and supports Apple Pay. The platform's daily revenue exceeds $400,000. shturl.c, Robinhood Chain, and Fomo all confirm one thing: regardless of market fluctuations, the market demand for Meme coins remains strong. Previously, participating in Meme Coin had a high barrier to entry: it required discovering opportunities in X and Telegram communities, using Dexscreener to query data, connecting your wallet to a DEX, and then executing trades. Participants were primarily users within the DeFi community. Now, with TikTok spreading Meme culture and the app supporting direct token purchases via Apple Pay, ordinary users outside the DeFi community can easily enter the market. The decline in traditional DeFi yields, coupled with the lowered entry barrier, has allowed Meme Coin to grow into a relatively independent sector less affected by overall market conditions. The image shows the monthly trading volume of prediction markets. Platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket drove the market to surge from almost negligible in 2024 to the $50 billion level by mid-2026, marking an explosive growth for the sector. Prediction markets were among the fastest-growing sectors in the past year: trading volume surged by 3032% year-on-year and 320% within the year, showing no signs of slowing down. Valuations of leading platforms continue to rise: Kalshi, valued at $750,000 in 2019, has reached $22 billion in May 2026 after multiple rounds of financing, with its next round of financing targeting $40 billion. Polymarket's valuation rose from $18.58 million in 2020 to $15 billion, with its new round of financing targeting over $20 billion. A comparison of the transaction structures of Polymarket and Kalshi using a dual-ring chart shows that sports are the largest transaction category in both platforms; Polymarket has a higher proportion of crypto and political themes, while Kalshi's sports themes account for 74.48%. When discussing market prediction in the industry, its ability to discover information and hedge risks is often mentioned, but currently, the actual demand for these two types of services is very limited. Kalshi's trading volume mainly comes from sports events and crypto market data; Polymarket has a wider range of categories, but its main trading focus remains on sports, crypto assets, and political events. Comparing the accumulated open interest of sports and weather contracts with different timeframes, weather contracts see large-scale position building early on, while sports contracts mostly accumulate positions rapidly closer to expiration. A comparison of weather and sports contracts reveals their differences: weather contract users open positions early, leaning towards hedging; sports contracts see large-scale trading concentrated closer to the event, essentially a speculative activity. The rapid expansion of prediction markets during bear markets is largely due to the influx of new users from outside the crypto space. Statistics show that 56.1% of wallet addresses on Polymarket have never interacted with a DEX. While this doesn't mean all users are complete newcomers to crypto, a large number use prediction markets as their first blockchain experience. Sports and political events help platforms transcend the crypto cycle and acquire new users from outside. [Image of perpetual contract decentralized exchanges] Comparing the trading volumes of the two types of DEXs, after 2025, the trading volume of perpetual DEXs (blue) has consistently exceeded that of spot DEXs (red), indicating significantly stronger demand for derivatives trading compared to spot trading. While perpetual contract DEXs haven't experienced the explosive growth of Meme Coin or prediction markets, their resilience in a bear market, compared to other on-chain data, is remarkably strong. The decline in trading volume for perpetual DEXs is far less than that for spot DEXs, indicating that speculative demand for contracts is stronger than that for spot trading. This is primarily driven by two factors: New perpetual contract protocols continue to emerge: Following the success of Hyperliquid, new projects such as Lighter, Aster, Variational, Grvt, and edgeX have launched one after another. Even companies that didn't previously focus on the contract market, like Jito, Jupiter, and Ondo Finance, have added perpetual contract products. The market has developed a "use new protocols to get airdrops" strategy, continuously attracting users to the sector. The Rise of Real-World Asset Perpetual Contracts (RWA-Perps): Previously, only BTC and ETH were available as underlying assets. Driven by geopolitical conflicts and the AI ​​sector, major platforms are now offering commodities and US stock-related contracts. For example, while it's difficult for ordinary investors outside of South Korea to trade SK Hynix stock, they can trade perpetual contracts for that stock on Hyperliquid, which once enjoyed extremely high trading volume. The concept of perpetual contracts originated with BitMEX. Although BitMEX itself declined and faced closure, the perpetual contract market continued to expand. Coinbase, Robinhood, Kalshi, and traditional compliant exchanges like the Singapore Exchange (SGX) and the US CME have all begun to develop similar trading products. Connecting to the Real Economy: Market growth is not entirely driven by speculation. On the other end of the barbell lies a sector with a somewhat rigid model but steady development, deeply integrated with the real world. Stablecoins, RWA (Real-World Asset Tokenization), and Vaults (asset treasuries) have maintained growth despite overall declines in token prices and on-chain staking. Venture capital investment in native on-chain projects has seen a significant contraction in both the number of projects and the scale of funding; however, blockchain projects integrated with the real economy are seeing increasingly larger single-round funding amounts. Examples include Rain's $250 million Series C funding, Airwallex's $320 million Series H funding, Gauntlet's $125 million funding, and OpenFX's $94 million funding. This demonstrates that this sector has successfully established independent product-market fit, unaffected by the cycles of crypto bull and bear markets.

Stablecoins

The white line represents the total market capitalization of stablecoins, which has remained relatively stable. However, the stacked bars represent the stablecoin payment transaction volume, which has continued to rise sharply, reflecting the shift in the focus of stablecoin applications towards actual payments.

Contrary to popular belief, the total supply of stablecoins has only increased by about 11% in the past year and has remained relatively flat since October 2025. The rapid expansion of government bond tokenization and private lending tokenization has slowed the growth rate of stablecoin supply.

But this does not mean that the sector is facing obstacles. In the context of a market crash, maintaining the existing size is an achievement in itself. More importantly, payment scenarios are experiencing explosive growth.

Crypto payment cards like RedotPay, KAST, EtherFi, and Plasma One saw their monthly payment volume nearly triple from $438.1 million in July 2025 to $1.32 billion in July 2026. Stablecoins, initially just intermediaries in crypto transactions, are increasingly being implemented in real-world payment scenarios. They will also serve as the core currency for on-chain settlement within the RWA real-world asset tokenization system. The total scale of real-world asset tokenization continues to rise, with traditional assets such as US Treasury bonds and commodities being the main contributors to growth. This expansion is independent of the cryptocurrency market cycle itself. 2025-2026 is expected to be a breakout year for RWA. The market anticipates blockchain technology transforming outdated traditional financial infrastructure, with various real-world assets being put on-chain. Early targets primarily consisted of US Treasury bonds and money market funds, with simple product forms and on-chain logic; later, this expanded to private lending, and recently further extended to stocks and equity. The value logic of RWA's underlying assets is independent of cryptocurrency market trends. Leveraging its advantages of increased efficiency and lower barriers to entry, it can grow independently of the crypto cycle. Four Pillars has already provided in-depth analysis of the RWA sector in previous reports, so this article will not repeat that. The line chart shows the TVL (Total Value Limit) trend of selected vaults. After a round of correction, it has rebounded again, approaching its previous historical peak, indicating that the popularity of institutional custody vaults has returned to a high level. Unlike RWA, which directly connects to real-world assets, Vaults are attracting significant industry attention as a next-generation on-chain asset management module. Vaults lend funds to lending markets that accept RWA as collateral, thereby indirectly linking with the real economy. As of August 28, the price of Bitcoin had fallen 35% from its peak; however, the total value locked in Select Vaults was only 4% lower than its all-time high, proving that the Vault ecosystem is also exhibiting independent market trends. Early RWA focused on "asset issuance on-chain"; now, as the industry enters the asset application stage, the rise of RWA-backed lending will further drive market demand for Vaults. Why are cryptocurrency companies no longer popular? The table summarizes the business layout of mainstream crypto platforms. △ represents ongoing development, ○ represents mature products, and - represents no involvement, reflecting the industry's expansion into emerging tracks such as perpetual contracts, prediction markets, RWA, and stablecoins. This has led to an intriguing business phenomenon in the crypto world: blockchain companies with completely different backgrounds and initial business focuses are now developing almost identical products and competing fiercely with each other. Various platforms are launching perpetual contracts, prediction markets, supporting Meme coin trading, and developing stablecoins, RWA trading, and asset vaults. The underlying logic is quite straightforward: as analyzed above, only a few tracks can both significantly mitigate market volatility and generate substantial revenue. Even with the recent market recovery, the overall direction of the industry hasn't changed, and many crypto companies are flocking to these counter-cyclical tracks. However, this doesn't mean that native on-chain projects have completely failed. While many experiments have disappeared as mentioned earlier, a few projects still survive and have successfully established a product-market fit. EigenLayer continues to see significant ETH re-staking; many are pessimistic about the blockchain gaming sector, but MapleStory Universe continues to deliver impressive data. The on-chain ecosystem is forming a barbell pattern. From a negative perspective: only a handful of sectors remain with growth potential; from a positive perspective: it represents the maturation of some crypto businesses, finding their own business models. We look forward to more sectors reaching this stage in the future.

data.title: What Happened to HTX’s 700 Million TRX? The Blockchain Trail Raises New Questions
data.description:
HTX moved roughly 700 million TRX out of a wallet it had previously identified as part of its reserves, shortly before the tokens disappeared from the exchange’s June proof-of-reserves disclosure.

At the prices cited in the investigation, the tokens were worth about $238 million.

Online sleuths are now providing some light on where those assets might have gone. A substantial portion seem to have reached an address that currently supports a Super Representative associated with Justin Sun’s Poloniex, while another 100 million TRX passed through HTX-linked wallets before reaching an address labeled as Binance-Hot 7.

The movements hence prove that the funds weren't stolen or misappropriated. However, it still raises fresh questions about how HTX manages and discloses its reserves — particularly as more than $1 billion in other assets were simultaneously moved under the control of an undisclosed “ThirdParty” custodian.

700 Million TRX Leaves an HTX Reserve Wallet

In May, HTX transferred 700 million TRX from an address labeled “HTX-Cold 6” that had previously appeared in the exchange’s proof-of-reserves. The 700 million TRX was later split between two main destinations.

About 200 million TRX was sent to TPznYuGCgYSWW8boAnFVMvv3RhNKqFaVpL before being forwarded to TFTWNgDBkQ5wQoP8RXpRznnHvAVV8x5jLu, an address identified as “HTX 4” on TronScan. The address HTX 4 had also appeared in the exchange’s proof-of-reserves, although it was later removed and was never shown as holding TRX in the disclosed assets.

Of those 200 million tokens, 180 million were subsequently transferred in two transactions to TEF9ZVUxhmGGffvkf59e2vdLfAG1QCMb7B, an otherwise unlabeled address. That wallet is now particularly notable because it votes roughly 928 million TRX for the Super Representative associated with Sun-owned Poloniex.

The remaining 500 million TRX followed a different route, moving to TT2T17KZhoDu47i2E4FWxfG79zdkEWkU9N, known as TT2. TT2 is one of the more controversial addresses in the investigation. Arkham Intelligence labels it “Justin Sun?” and the wallet is a significant redeemer of TrueUSD, the stablecoin with longstanding ties to Sun’s crypto empire. The address has also previously delegated energy to HTX 4.

孙哥 Justin Sun 在 5 小时前将 1.1 亿枚 USDT 转进 HTX。
哥，要继续抄底 ETH 吗🤔

◎通过 TT2...U9N 地址从 JustLend 取回 6510 万 USDT，然后将 7000 万 USDT 转进 HTX；https://t.co/zUvY2lO3jJ

◎通过 0xdbf...ec8 地址从 Aave 取回 4024 万 USDT，然后转进 HTX。https://t.co/4yXEDWxBNc… pic.twitter.com/BYrXSAkXHa

— 余烬 (@EmberCN) August 3, 2024

That does not prove that Sun controls TT2. Sun also seem to been evasive when questioned by Bloomberg about the wallet’s ownership.

The Money Trail Also Leads Toward Binance

The movement of the 500 million TRX becomes even more interesting when looking at TT2’s transactions immediately before the funds arrived. One day before receiving the 500 million TRX from the HTX reserve wallet, TT2 sent 100 million TRX to TEgMTsmbVbjGK9bSeEjkZmcE8EFW8iJ8RT.

That wallet immediately forwarded the funds to HTX 4. From there, the TRX moved to TGPeN3mRTtYaAPvkPH2RJYwUQVcjYvMRS3 and then to TDqSquXBgUCLYvYC4XZgrprLK589dkhSCf, an address TronScan labels “Binance-Hot 7.”

According to Cyvers Alerts, suspicious address has received $12.4M from HTX exchange and suspicious address has received around $85M from HECO Chain bridge. HTX and HECO are Justin Sun's business. Justin Sun’s Poloniex has just been stolen for more than $100 million.…

— Wu Blockchain (@WuBlockchain) November 22, 2023

In other words, an HTX-linked wallet appears to have sent 100 million TRX toward a Binance hot wallet just before TT2 received 500 million TRX that had originated from HTX’s disclosed reserves. Another 180 million TRX followed a similarly complicated path.

TT2 sent the tokens to TBRoa9xabNSTXTSK6iQAMPQQ7CNo2j2yuF, which quickly forwarded them to HTX 4. HTX 4 then transferred the funds in two transactions to TEF9, the address currently voting for the Poloniex Super Representative. HTX 4 also sent 35 million TRX back to TT2, creating a partial loop in the flow of funds.

The pattern resembles the movement of stETH that was previously tracked leaving HTX, including the use of short-lived addresses that briefly handled funds before forwarding them elsewhere.

Taken together, the transactions show millions of dollars in TRX moving through a network of HTX-linked, unlabeled and exchange-associated addresses.

But they still leave a central question unanswered: why did HTX move the 700 million TRX out of its disclosed reserve wallet in the first place?

HTX’s Reserve Transparency Faces New Scrutiny

The question carries more weight because the TRX movement was not the only major change in HTX’s June proof-of-reserves.

In the same disclosure that showed the roughly 700 million TRX reduction, HTX also reduced its reported holdings of more than $1 billion worth of other assets, instead attributing them to an undisclosed “ThirdParty” custodian.

JUST IN: Chinese crypto billionaire Justin Sun accused of paying a $4.5 million “bride fee” to marry actress Jing Tian, then trying to claw it back after the relationship collapsed. pic.twitter.com/HiYbe5bLLT

— Polymarket (@Polymarket) September 14, 2026

Online sleuths had previously tracked a substantial portion of HTX’s Ethereum reserves to Poloniex, adding another layer to questions surrounding how assets move between companies and wallets associated with Sun’s broader crypto empire.

At the same time, HTX has since been sanctioned by the European Union and the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office, making questions about where the exchange’s assets are held — and who ultimately controls them — more consequential.

The 700 million TRX represents less than 10% of HTX’s total disclosed TRX holdings. The exchange’s latest disclosure still reports roughly 9.3 billion TRX, including about 922 million TRX currently lent through JustLend.

So the blockchain trail does not show that HTX has lost $238 million in TRX.

What it does show is something potentially more important for an exchange operating under growing regulatory scrutiny: hundreds of millions of dollars in previously disclosed reserves moved through a web of wallets that includes addresses tied to HTX, a Poloniex-associated Super Representative and Binance, while the exchange simultaneously changed how it disclosed more than $1 billion in other assets.

The transactions provide part of the answer to where HTX’s TRX went. They do not yet provide the answer to why.

data.title: TikTok Parent ByteDance Secures $29.6 Billion Loan From 28 Banks To Fund Major AI Expansion
data.description:
ByteDance is turning to the debt market to help fund its growing artificial intelligence ambitions, securing $29.6 billion from a group of 28 banks after lenders showed stronger-than-expected appetite for the deal.

ByteDance Secures $29.6 Billion AI Loan

The three-year unsecured facility was coordinated by Citigroup and JPMorgan, with the borrowing later expandable to as long as five years.

ByteDance had initially sought $20 billion, but increased the facility after commitments from lenders exceeded the original target.

The deal is one of Asia’s largest dollar-denominated corporate borrowings in 2026, ranking second behind SoftBank’s $40 billion bridge loan linked to its investment in OpenAI.

📢 𝗝𝗨𝗦𝗧 𝗜𝗡: ByteDance Secures $𝟮𝟵.𝟲 Billion Loan as AI Investment Accelerates

👉 𝗞𝗲𝘆 𝗛𝗶𝗴𝗵𝗹𝗶𝗴𝗵𝘁𝘀:

➤ 𝗕𝘆𝘁𝗲𝗗𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 secured a $𝟮𝟵.𝟲 billion loan from nearly 𝟯𝟬 banks.

➤ Financing is reportedly Asia's 𝘀𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗱-𝗹𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗲𝘀𝘁 loan this year.…

— Hardik Shah (@AIStockSavvy) September 4, 2026

The scale of the financing gives ByteDance more funding capacity as it spends heavily on AI computing, chips and data centre infrastructure.

Why Did Banks Back The Larger Loan?

The financing attracted 28 banks, including major Chinese and international lenders.

Chinese banks accounted for the largest share, committing a combined $18.9 billion, or about 64% of the total facility.

Industrial and Commercial Bank of China agreed to provide $3 billion, while Bank of China committed $2.5 billion and China Construction Bank provided $1.5 billion.

HSBC and two other foreign banks each committed $1.5 billion.

The loan is also notable because it is unsecured, meaning ByteDance did not pledge specific assets as collateral.

One source involved in the financing said,

"It is very rare to see such a mega loan unsecured.”

"The banks practically are counting purely on ByteDance's name."

The facility carries an opening margin of 68 basis points above the Secured Overnight Financing Rate, a relatively low borrowing cost compared with SoftBank’s March facility, which had an initial margin of about 250 basis points.

AI Investment Drives ByteDance’s Funding Needs

ByteDance has not provided a detailed breakdown of how the new financing will be spent, with the loan formally intended for general corporate purposes.

However, people familiar with the financing said AI investment is a major reason behind the company’s increased funding needs.

The company has been expanding its Seed AI research division, which was established in 2023 and works on foundation models and other AI systems.

ByteDance has also developed Doubao, along with AI models covering language, images, video and audio.

Building and running these systems requires large amounts of computing power, pushing ByteDance to secure additional chips and data centre capacity.

Some of the financing is expected to support AI chips and data centres outside China, including projects in Southeast Asia.

ByteDance is reportedly acting as a customer for several overseas data centre projects, although specific sites, construction schedules and spending commitments have not been publicly confirmed.

bytedance just secured $29.6b from 28 banks for its overseas ai buildout...

that's a pretty good reminder that the ai startup race isn't only about who has the smartest model

someone has to pay for the data centres, gpus and computing capacity behind all of it..and when a… pic.twitter.com/eegE3zeqDO

— Jules Solopreneur (@julian_soloship) September 14, 2026

ByteDance Could Spend Up To $70 Billion On AI Infrastructure

The new loan comes as ByteDance considers a much larger AI spending programme.

Bloomberg reported in May that the company was considering capital spending of as much as $70 billion during 2026, covering data centres and other AI infrastructure.

The figure was described as a potential spending ceiling rather than a confirmed investment budget, and ByteDance has not publicly confirmed the amount.

ByteDance, the developer of TikTok, is planning to sharply increase its capital spending this year and next in a bid to lead the Chinese AI market and challenge top US players https://t.co/D6CL3WUaF4

— Bloomberg (@business) May 27, 2026

The company has also faced rising costs and supply constraints as it expands its computing capacity.

US export controls restrict access to certain advanced processors and related components, while shortages of high-bandwidth memory have increased costs for Chinese AI chip suppliers.

These restrictions have made access to computing resources both inside and outside China an important part of ByteDance’s AI strategy.

China’s Tech Giants Race To Build AI Computing Power

ByteDance’s borrowing places it alongside Alibaba and Tencent as Chinese technology companies pour money into AI infrastructure.

The spending increasingly resembles the huge capital programmes undertaken by major US technology companies, particularly around data centres and computing hardware.

For ByteDance, the investment comes despite pressure on profitability.

Its net profit fell by more than 70% in 2025, with the company partly attributing the decline to accounting changes, while the scale of its AI investment has also increased costs.

The latest loan gives the privately held company additional debt funding without requiring it to sell equity.

ByteDance previously raised $10.8 billion through a loan involving about 20 banks in 2024, making the latest facility nearly three times larger.

The latest financing also comes as ByteDance competes with global AI companies while acknowledging that its large language models trail leading systems developed by companies such as OpenAI and Google.

data.title: Why are long-term interest rates unwilling to fall?
data.description: The Treasury continues to expand the scale of national debt issuance, while the Federal Reserve is gradually withdrawing from its role as a major buyer through balance sheet reduction. Given the continued increase in the supply of long-term national debt, who will absorb this new debt? The most noteworthy phenomenon in the global financial markets over the past year has not been whether major central banks have entered a rate-cutting cycle, but rather why long-term interest rates remain high despite rate cuts. Based on decades of experience, a decline in policy rates usually leads to a simultaneous downward shift in the entire yield curve. However, this cycle presents a different picture. Since September 2024, the Federal Reserve has cumulatively cut interest rates by 175 basis points, yet the yields on 10-year and 30-year US Treasury bonds have risen significantly. Investors are willing to believe that short-term interest rates will eventually fall, but are no longer willing to hold government bonds at extremely low yields for the long term as they have in the past. This phenomenon, seemingly a mere technical adjustment within the bond market, actually reflects a deeper pricing shift in global capital markets. For the past two decades, whether it was the bursting of the dot-com bubble, the global financial crisis, or the impact of the pandemic, the market has consistently believed in a fundamental logic: once the economy faces pressure, central banks will eventually lower financing costs by cutting interest rates, and long-term interest rates will return to lower levels. Long-term government bonds have therefore been not only safe-haven assets but also important anchors for the valuation of various assets such as stocks, real estate, and corporate bonds. However, today, signals from the bond market are challenging this long-standing consensus. The market's focus has gradually shifted from "when will the next interest rate cut come?" to "who will ultimately bear the burden of the government's ever-expanding debt?" Looking at the US Treasury market, the recent rise in long-term interest rates is not primarily due to runaway inflation expectations. During the yield increase, the contribution of the term premium is significantly higher than that of inflation expectations themselves. The so-called term premium is essentially the additional compensation that investors demand for holding long-term bonds. In other words, the market is no longer only worried about whether prices will rise in the future, but also about the uncertainty of fiscal policy, debt supply, and the political environment over the next ten, twenty, or even thirty years. The role of long-term government bonds is changing. In the past, investors viewed them more as natural safe-haven assets, their value primarily reflecting economic growth and inflation expectations; now, the market is increasingly focused on the long-term sustainability of public finances, so long-term government bonds are no longer just a safe-haven tool, but are gradually becoming a type of long-term investment asset requiring additional risk compensation. Behind this change is a systemic shift in the fiscal landscape of developed economies. The massive fiscal stimulus during the pandemic pushed the debt levels of most major economies to historical highs. After the pandemic, the market expected fiscal deficits to gradually return to normal, but reality has not followed this path. Whether it's industrial policy, green transformation, expansion of defense spending, or the increased pension and healthcare costs brought about by population aging, all indicate that government spending will remain high for a considerable period. Meanwhile, the political constraints of fiscal discipline are weakening, making deficit reduction increasingly difficult. The situation in the United States is most representative. As the Treasury continues to expand the scale of national debt issuance, and the Federal Reserve gradually withdraws from its role as a major buyer through balance sheet reduction, the market is forced to confront an increasingly important question: with the continuous increase in the supply of long-term government bonds, who will absorb this new debt? This problem is not unique to the United States, but a challenge faced by the global bond market. For the past two decades, Japan has been one of the most important sources of funds for the global bond market. The ultra-low interest rate environment prompted Japanese insurance institutions, pension funds, and banks to allocate large amounts of overseas bonds, providing stable buying power for the European and American bond markets. However, in recent years, Japan's interest rate level has gradually normalized, domestic bond yields have continued to rise, and the cost of currency hedging remains high, significantly reducing the attractiveness of allocating long-term overseas bonds. For the European and American markets, this means that a long-term stable marginal buyer is weakening, and the international capital flow pattern that was once taken for granted is changing. Similar signals have emerged in the European market. The 2022 turmoil in the UK gilt market was considered an exceptional event, but it reflected the same underlying issue: when fiscal expansion, increased debt supply, and persistent inflation occur simultaneously, long-term bond investors demand higher risk compensation. The recent surge in French bond yields above Italian bond yields sends a more symbolic signal to the market. This does not signify a return of the European debt crisis, but rather indicates that investors are reassessing the fiscal creditworthiness of different countries within the Eurozone. For a long time, France has almost naturally been considered a core country in the Eurozone, but the market is increasingly pricing based on fiscal condition rather than traditional status. The scope of the bond market's assessment of fiscal risk has gradually expanded from peripheral countries to core countries. Compared to the two famous bond bear markets of 1994 and 2022, the current rise in long-term interest rates has a significantly different nature. The 1994 adjustment was primarily driven by the Federal Reserve's rapid interest rate hikes, while the 2022 adjustment was forced by an inflationary shock that compelled major central banks to tighten monetary policy at an unprecedented pace. Both rounds of adjustments began with a sharp rise in short-term interest rates. Today, the situation is exactly the opposite: the Federal Reserve has entered a rate-cutting cycle, and pressure on short-term interest rates is easing, but long-term yields remain high. This means that the two ends of the yield curve are beginning to reflect different types of risk: the short end reflects more the direction of monetary policy, while the long end is increasingly affected by changes in fiscal deficits, debt supply, and term premiums. The market logic of "central banks dominating everything" that has formed over the past few decades is being gradually corrected. This is precisely why the current market exhibits a rather subtle split. On the one hand, the US stock market is near historical highs, the investment boom in artificial intelligence continues, and corporate bond credit spreads remain relatively low, indicating that investors' risk appetite has not weakened significantly. On the other hand, long-term Treasury yields remain high, indicating that the bond market maintains a stronger cautious attitude towards the future. Bond investors are actually sending an important signal: if the long-term risk-free rate cannot return to its low levels of the past decade, all assets relying on low discount rates and cheap financing will face revaluation. High valuations themselves do not necessarily mean a bubble, but the long-term coexistence of high valuations and high financing costs will significantly reduce the market's tolerance for mistakes and risks. This is particularly noteworthy in the field of artificial intelligence infrastructure investment. Data centers, computing networks, power systems, and communication infrastructure undoubtedly constitute one of the most important capital expenditure directions in the coming years. From a demand perspective, the investment wave brought about by artificial intelligence continues to expand. However, unlike many previous technology cycles, these projects are often characterized by huge investment scales, long construction cycles, and strong financing needs. In an era of ultra-low interest rates, the cost of capital is often not the key variable determining the success or failure of a project; however, in an environment where long-term interest rates remain high, the financing structure itself may determine the final rate of return. Large technology companies can support capital expenditures with strong cash flow, while operators who rely more on debt financing have to face higher capital costs. Therefore, judging the sustainability of AI investment requires not only considering the rate of demand growth but also the alignment between project cash flow, debt maturity, and financing costs. Looking at a longer historical period, the global financial market may be bidding farewell to an era that lasted for over three decades. From the 1990s until the outbreak of the pandemic, deepening globalization, continuous technological progress, demographic changes, and relatively restrained fiscal policies collectively drove long-term interest rates downward. The market gradually formed an almost self-evident belief: long-term capital would become increasingly cheaper. However, reality is changing. Geopolitical competition is driving increased defense spending, industrial policies are resurging, green transitions require massive investments, an aging population is creating sustained fiscal pressure, and a democratic political environment is making fiscal austerity increasingly difficult. Central banks can still determine overnight interest rates, but they are finding it increasingly difficult to determine the price of capital over the next few decades. In this sense, the current rise in long-term interest rates is not merely a bond market adjustment, but rather a repricing of the "fiscal state" by investors. Government bond yields no longer reflect only the prospects for economic growth and inflation, but also the market's judgment on the government's long-term debt repayment capacity, fiscal discipline, and policy credibility. The most important macroeconomic issue in the coming years may no longer be when the next interest rate cut will occur, but whether major economies can reassure the market that their ever-expanding debt remains on a sustainable track. When the market begins to doubt this premise, long-term government bond yields are often the first to react. However, rising yields are not the end point; they will eventually be transmitted to the broader financial system through changes in financing costs, asset valuations, and credit conditions. Therefore, changes in long-term interest rates are not only an internal issue of the bond market, but also an important window for observing the future direction of global economic and financial order adjustments.
